fragments.text: Hello, my name is Camille Stewart Gloucester and I am the CEO of CIS strategies and emerging technology and cyber security firm in the United States. I had the honor of serving as the first deputy national cyber director focused on technology and ecosystem security at the White House under President Biden and vice president Harris. In that role, I was tasked to focus on emerging technologies like AI and quantum and convergence of those. Supply chain security, privacy, human rights and technology, cyber workforce, the portfolio was very future resilience focused. We painted an affirmative vision for what we want a future digital ecosystem to look like. It would be values aligned and something we all can share and be secure, defensible, resilient and equitable.
fragments.summary: Hello, my name is Camille Stewart Gloucester and I am the CEO of CIS strategies and emerging technology and cyber security firm in the United States.

fragments.text: And if we are to achieve that desired end, how do we look at the technologies that we have today? In the lessons we have learned from the innovations of the past, I apply that to what is coming down the pipeline and to the functions and enabling capabilities that allow for technological innovation and the technology that is working for us in these times. And so through that lens and my experience in industry and academia, I think about how we can make sure that AI innovation is working for us. And we're doing a lot of that work. You've seen secure by design, privacy by design, product inclusion with its focus on how to make sure people are seen in technological innovation, take hold as companies and governments promote aligning values early in the lifecycle of a technological innovation.
fragments.summary: And if we are to achieve that desired end, how do we look at the technologies that we have today?

fragments.text: Those frameworks incorporate our values from the very beginning by thinking about the risks ahead and trying to mitigate those risks so that we can realize the full opportunity and benefit of technology. What I'm excited to see is that as AI innovation and particularly the public awareness of and industry investment in generative AI moves forward, we are having the right conversations to start to build out governance structures that serve our collective and shared goals to think about interoperability and how we build out a trustworthy AI capability. And capability that contemplates security, safety, privacy up front, mitigates bias, protects us from harms like human rights violations. So we are thinking critically about those things. That's an exciting and important evolution of our shared investment in leveraging the tooling capability that is technology.
fragments.summary: Those frameworks incorporate our values from the very beginning by thinking about the risks ahead and trying to mitigate those risks so that we can realize the full opportunity and benefit of technology.

fragments.text: Because technology is amplification mechanism, it will amplify the best and worst of what we bring to it. And so taking the time to mitigate the potential harms and risks and threats associated with technology is our shared duty. What I have seen though is that we seek to make as much change as possible in a short time, whether it is incremental or large scale. But to truly have sustained impact and to be able to evolve with the changing technological dynamics and to meet the moment on cultivating a global AI innovation ethos and ecosystem that aligns to our values and that meets the goals and demands that we have as a global society, we must make a couple long-term investments that will take a lot of resources, a lot of time, but are so worth it.

fragments.text: Because the way that they underpin and accelerate our goals means that they must, must, must be made a priority. But sometimes long-term investments fall on the back burner or we make very small changes rather than the whole scale investments that are necessary to truly make meaningful change in that area. And two areas stand to mind or come to mind. Education, we need to revamp and retool our education systems to meet the moment. There are a lot of technology jobs left unfilled and as innovation continues to grow, there will only be more need for those that are technologically savvy and can fill open roles that facilitate technology being a service to each of us. But in addition to that, there are a set of skills that we almost have to move through a technologically enabled world.

fragments.text: And so it will fuel innovation. It will spur economic opportunity. It will embed the values we want to see in our technology by empowering and enable each individual to be a meaningful part of the discourse. So we must invest in education and revamping our education system and that is a shared challenge. There is no nation that does not need to make that investment. And then the second is really thinking about a global investment infrastructure. There has been a lot of conversation about it being a fund and access to compute and compute credits and making sure that the infrastructure is there, but it is not one of those things. It is all of those things. Whatever this global investment infrastructure turns out to be will require us to have financial investment from companies, governments alike, but also intellectual investments and infrastructure investments that allow for AI innovation hubs to develop across the world.
fragments.summary: It will embed the values we want to see in our technology by empowering and enable each individual to be a meaningful part of the discourse.

There are a lot of conversations having a number of multilateral bodies that think that are thinking through how we spur that investment infrastructure and the finances to do this work. And so continued investment and thinking about new models and new infrastructure investments that allow for this unlocking is going to be integral.
